PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND
On March 16, 2026, after completing mediation, the Redwood City School
District (District) filed a request for factfinding pursuant to the Educational Employment
Relations Act (EERA)1 with the Public Employment Relations Board (PERB) regarding
its negotiations with the California School Employees Association and its Chapter 5
(CSEA) regarding the reduction of hours of Library Media Technical Associate (LMTA)
and Library Media Assistant (LMA) positions at the District’s school library sites.2
On March 16 and 18, 2026, the parties selected their factfinding panel
members and on April 20, 2026, PERB notified the undersigned arbitrator that he had
been selected as the Chair of the factfinding panel.
On May 6, 2026,3 the Chair held an organizational meeting where the agenda
of the factfinding proceeding, factfinding proceeding dates, options for closing
arguments, and the issuance date of the factfinding report and recommendation(s) for
settlement (factfinding report) were discussed. The parties agreed that the factfinding
1 EERA is codified at Government Code section 3540 et seq.

increase or reduction in hours of LMTAs and LMAs at five of the eleven District school
library sites. This factfinding report will focus on the six remaining individual school
library sites that the parties could not come to an agreement as to the reduction in
hours of LMTAs/LMAs: Adelante Selby School, Garfield School, Hoover School,
Roy Cloud School, Clifford School and McKinley Institute of Technology/North Star
Academy (MIT/North Star).
3 On April 21, 2026, CSEA had notified the Chair that the parties had agreed to
extend the statutory time frames regarding the factfinding proceeding. (Government

uncontested facts section contained in this factfinding report.
2

proceeding would be scheduled for May 19 and 20, 2026; the parties would be
submitting oral closing arguments on May 20, 2026; and the factfinding report would
be issued on June 3, 2026.
The factfinding proceeding was held and concluded on May 19 and 20, 2026.
Both parties presented arguments/exhibits surrounding the issues in dispute. Both
parties made closing arguments at the end of their cases-in-chief rather than at the
end of both parties’ presentations. On May 22, 2026, the Chair asked the parties for
the District’s job descriptions for both the LMTA and the LMA positions and the
District’s Fiscal Stabilization Plan mentioned in one of the slides of its presentation.
Neither party objected to the documents being provided to the Chair and the panel
and the District provided these documents to the entire panel and CSEA.
STATEMENT OF THE ISSUE
The parties were able to jointly stipulate to the issue in this matter which was:
Should the weekly hours (and resulting full-time equivalency – FTE) of
certain classified Library Media Assistants and Library Media [Technical]
Associates be reduced?
FACTFINDING CRITERIA
EERA provides statutory criteria in Government Code section 3548.2,
subd. (b)(1) through (7), for the factfinding panel to consider, weigh, and be guided by
in determining findings and recommendations. Those statutory criteria are:
“(b) In arriving at their findings and recommendations, the factfinders
shall consider, weigh, and be guided by all the following criteria:
“(1) State and federal laws that are applicable to the employer.
“(2) Stipulations of the parties.
3

“(3) The interests and welfare of the public and the financial
ability of the public school employer.
“(4) Comparison of the wages, hours, and conditions of
employment of the employees involved in the factfinding
proceeding with the wages, hours, and conditions of
employment of other employees performing similar services
and with other employees generally in public school
employment in comparable communities.
“(5) The consumer price index for goods and services,
commonly known as the cost of living.
“(6) The overall compensation presently received by the
employees, including direct wage compensation, vacations,
holidays, and other excused time, insurance and pensions,
medical and hospitalization benefits; the continuity and stability
of employment; and all other benefits received.
“(7) Any other facts, not confined to those specified in
paragraphs (1) to (6), inclusive, which are normally or
traditionally taken into consideration in making the findings and
recommendations.
Of these factfinding factors, the parties agreed that the statutory criteria listed in
Government Code section 3548.2, subd. (b)(4), was inapplicable to this factfinding
proceeding.
FINDINGS OF FACT
Stipulations of Uncontested Facts between the Parties
The parties agreed to the following pertinent uncontested facts in this matter:
“1. [The District] is a public school employer within the meaning of
Government Code section 3540.1(k) of [EERA].
“2. CSEA and its Redwood City Chapter [5] is a recognized employee
organization within the meaning of Government Code
4

section 3540.1(1) of [EERA] and has been duly recognized as the
representative of the classified non-management bargaining unit[.]
“3. The parties have complied with [EERA] with regard to the selection
of the Factfinding Panel and have met or waived the statutory time
limitations applicable to this proceeding.
“4. The District has complied with section 5.1.4 of the parties’ collective
bargaining agreement which provides:
“When the District needs to increase or decrease the hours of a
bargaining unit position it should provide written notice and an
opportunity to bargain to CSEA.”
Background
The District is a public school employer which educates students from
prekindergarten through the eighth grade. Generally, the individual schools within the
-
Districts employ LMTAs and LMAs who provide library media services to the students
attending those schools within the District. Usually, a singular LMTA or an LMA is
assigned to an individual school site library and reports to the district librarian and the
school site principal:
The job description for LMTA provides in pertinent part:
“REPRESENTATIVE DUTIES
“[ . . . ]
“1. Assist with the training and professional development of school
library media assistants, particularly in the areas of new and/or
upgrades of software programs such as . . . which are necessary for
the smooth functioning of Redwood City School District's Library
Media Centers. This will include attending training sessions with
the technology department and organizing and presenting
workshops for [LMAs] in newly adopted software programs.
5

“2. Provide troubleshooting services for software and equipment and
initiate help tickets for equipment that needs to be repaired by the
Technology Department.
“3. Communicate to [LMAs] various methods and techniques used for
machine readable cataloging [(MARC)], MARC records, budget
monitoring using Excel, library program activities, lesson planning,
and presentations using PowerPoint or overheads.
“4. Serve as a mentor to a designated group of [LMAs].
“5. Provide exemplary library media service and programming in the
following areas:
“● Organize and maintain the routine operation of a school library
media center including maintenance and weeding of the
collection; receive, process, circulate and shelve print and
non-print materials according to accepted library procedures.
“● Assist teachers in teaching students basic information literacy
skills; i.e., access, use and evaluate print and non-print
materials to improve literacy.
“● Assist students and teachers in locating and selecting
appropriate materials; assist students with special class theme
projects or conduct story time as required.
“● Maintain routine records related to library activities including
circulation of books, monies collected and lost materials.
“● Schedule library media times for classes. Train, assign and
monitor work of volunteer and student helpers.
“● Maintain the library media center in a clean and orderly
condition providing an environment conducive to learning and
literacy; assist in maintaining the discipline of students.
6

“● Create displays to promote reading and library media units and
themes.
(Bolding included in quotation.)
The job description for the LMA provides in pertinent part:
“REPRESENTATIVE DUTIES:
“Organize and maintain the routine operation of a school library media
center including maintenance and weeding of the collection; receive,
process, circulate and shelve print and non-print materials according to
magnet theme.
“Assist teachers in teaching students basic information literacy skills; i.e.:
access, use and evaluate print and non-print materials to improve
literacy through the magnet theme.
“Assist students and teachers in locating and selecting appropriate
materials; assist students with special class magnet theme projects or
conduct story time as required.
“Maintain routine records related to library activities including circulation
of books, monies collected and lost materials.
“Schedule library media times for classes. Train, assign and monitor
work of volunteer and student helpers.
“Maintain the library media center in a clean and orderly condition
providing an environment conducive to learning and literacy; assist in
maintaining the discipline of students.
“Create displays to promote reading and library media units and magnet
theme.”
(Bolding included in quotation.)
A full-time equivalent LMTA/LMA is scheduled to work 37.5 hours per week.
The 37.5-hour week includes 2.5 hours in paid breaks a week (two 15-minute breaks
7

per day) and a half-hour daily unpaid lunch period.4 In general, the school site
libraries have schedules in which individual grade classes come to their libraries for
half-hour periods—usually from Monday to Wednesday and Friday. Thursday is
usually a day when the LMTAs and LMAs meet with each other and the district
librarian once a month for a limited period of time. Thursday is also the workday on
which LMTAs/LMAs complete their assigned tasks which do not involve hosting a
class of students in the school site library.5
The hours of operation of the library at the six remaining school library sites
varied, even if the LMTA/LMA was scheduled to work 37.5 hours a week. The
Adelante Selby School library operated from 7:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. The Hoover and
Clifford School libraries operated from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. The Roy Cloud School
library operated from 8:00 a.m. to 2:45 p.m. The Garfield School library operated from
8:10 a.m. to 3:45 p.m. Lastly, the MIT/North Star Library operated from 8:30 a.m. to
4:00 p.m.6
At the District, LMTAs are compensated at pay grade 25.5 ($35.25 to $44.94 an
hour) while LMAs are compensated at pay grade 19.5 ($26.23 to $33.56 an hour).
4 Some LMTAs and LMAs work less than 37.5 hours a week.
5 For the six remaining library school sites in question for which agreements to
a reduction in hours could not be achieved, one site (the Hoover School library)
hosted student classes on Thursdays, but the general practice according to the school
site library schedules was that the LMTAs and LMAs used Thursday to perform their
duties which did not involve hosting a class of students or the preparation involved
with hosting that class.
6 MIT/North Star shared the same library. The LMTA/LMA who worked at the
MIT/North Star library worked 35 hours a week.
8

The primary difference between the two classifications, LMTA and LMA, is that the
LMTA position requires the completion of a Library Media Technology certificate or the
completion of a library media program accredited from a college, which then required
the LMTA to complete additional duties.
Declining Enrollment
The District has experienced a continuing trend of declining student enrollment
over the last ten school years. From school year 2015-20167 to 2024-2025, student
enrollment at the District has declined from 8,414 to 6,409 students8—a decline of
2,005 students, or a 24 percent reduction in students. In school year 2018-2019, the
District had to close four of its schools due to declining student enrollment.
Fiscal Stabilization Plan
On December 11, 2024, the Superintendent recommended for approval to the
District Board a Budget Renewal Initiative which proposed to save the District
$6.6 million dollars to address the expiration of one-time federal and state pandemic
relief funds and ensure the District’s long-term financial stability.9 The cost-saving
proposals which the Superintendent recommended to the District Board included:
7 The 2015-2016 school year was the last school year in which the District
determined its staffing and weekly hour allotment of LMTAs/LMAs to individual school
sites. On March 7, 2016, the District and CSEA agreed to an increased allotment of
hours for LMTAs/LMAs at various individual school sites.
8 Unfortunately for the District, its current student enrollment and
projected student enrollment continue to decline. The District student enrollment
for school year 2025-2026 was 6,309 students and the anticipated District student
enrollment for school year 2026-2027 is 6,100 students.
9 This initiative later became known as the Fiscal Stabilization Plan.
9

(1) reducing seven district and school site administrator positions; (2) reducing five
district office positions; (3) reducing funding to specific school sites; (4) reducing the
hours of LMTAs/LMAs at nine schools and increasing the hours of LMTAs/LMAs at
two schools due to the overall declining student enrollment; (5) reducing the hours of
13 paraeducators and eliminating two contracted positions within the District’s Special
Education Department.
The District Board agenda item for Proposal 4 regarding the reduction/increase
of LMTAs/LMAs hours at eleven school library sites provided:
“Superintendent Recommendation #4: Adjust Staffing Due to
Ongoing Declining Enrollment
“Proposal: Address staffing due to projected enrollment fluctuations for
2025-[2026], for a savings of approximately $200,000
“● Adjust hours for [LMTAs] at nine schools (reductions) and two schools
(increases).
“● Reduce office staff hours
“● Conduct an analysis of classroom staffing needs.
“Rationale: Although [transitional kindergarten] expansion has stabilized overall
districtwide enrollment numbers during the last three school years, we continue
to see families with students in all grade levels leaving the Bay Area and the
state. While the community disagreed with reductions related to enrollment
(56 [percent] to 44 [percent]), district demographers continue to study our area,
which shows an ongoing decline each year with approximately 1,000 fewer
students by 2033-[2034].”
(Bolding and underlining included in quotation.)
Notice to Bargain Reduction in Hours of LMTAs/LMAs
On March 12, 2025, the District provided CSEA with notice that it intended to
reduce the hours of the LMTA and LMA positions due to the District’s lack of funds
and lack of work resulting from declining student reenrollment.. The notice included a
10

spreadsheet which indicated the proposed reduction in weekly hours to the specific
LMTA/LMA positions at specific school site libraries and stated that the reductions
were to take effect at the beginning of the 2025-2026 school year. The parties
bargained regarding these proposed changes to LMTAs/LMAs weekly hours at the
eleven school library sites. The parties were able to come to agreements as to a
reduction/increase in weekly hours at five of the eleven school library sites.
Reduction in Work and Final Bargaining Proposals
The District’s contention that the LMTAs/LMAs had less work to perform is
based upon the extraneous preparation time which LMTAs/LMAs had in their weekly
schedules. In a sense, in attempting to right-size the hours of the LMTAs/LMAs, the
District focused on the essential duties of LMTAs/LMAs as to (1) the amount of
individual class student time (half-hour increment classes) which came to a school
library site a week, (2) half-hour preparatory periods for each half-hour increment of
individual class time, (3) lunch periods where the LMTA/LMA hosted students, and
(4) additional LMTA/LMA preparation time allotted to the library’s program design (the
Thursday workday where LMTAs/LMAs completed their assignments set forth in their
job descriptions which were not related to students being presence.)
The following table represents the LMTAs/LMAs essential duty information
regarding the allotted weekly hours for the six remaining school library sites as taken
from the schedules of the individual library school sites:

In addition to the District’s proposal regarding its hourly reductions to the
LMTAs/LMAs weekly schedules, it proposed an effective date of January 1, 2026 for
the implementation of this reduction. Additionally, the District proposed that all of the
LMTAs/LMAs at these six individual school sites would continue to receive full-time
equivalent employee health insurance benefits as long as the employee remained in
their assigned LMTA/LMA position at their school library site.
CSEA argues that its last proposal still saves the District $83,828.00 while the
District’s proposals save the District $142,952.00. The difference in cost savings
between the two proposals was $59,124.00. In reviewing the District’s unrestricted
general fund budget reserves in the 2025-2026 school year Second Interim Financial
Report,12 CSEA contends that the District has the financial ability to pay this
differential of cost savings as the District has $11,563,122.21 in cash reserves.
Deep Hourly Reductions to Incumbent LMTAs/LMAs and the Consumer Price Index
CSEA contends that the District’s September 17, 2025 last, best and final
proposal imposes deep hourly reductions to LMTAs/LMAs which create significant
financial hardships for the LMTAs/LMAs. The LMTAs/LMAs at Garfield School,
Adelante Selby School and MIT/North Start will experience a reduction in hours at
37 percent, 20 percent and 18 percent, respectively. On top of these reductions,
these same employees will lose an additional 3.8 percent of purchasing power as a
result of the consumer price index (CPI). (See Western Region CPI for April 2026.)
12 This Second Interim Financial Report sets forth the actual revenues and
expenditures of the District up to January 31, 2026.
13

CSEA asserts that such deep reductions will only result in future negative implications
as to the recruitment and retention of LMTAs/LMAs for the District.
APPLICATION OF STATUTORY CRITERIA AND RECOMMENDATIONS
Unlike interest arbitration, where a third-party neutral sets the terms of a
new agreement, a third-party neutral in an EERA factfinding report simply provides
recommendation(s) as to terms for settlement, which shall be advisory only.
(Gov. Code, § 3548.3, subd. (a).) In essence, the impasse resolution procedure,
which includes the factfinding process, is a continuation of the collective bargaining
process. (Regents of the University of California (2026) PERB Decision No. 3010-H,
p. 5; San Bernardino County Superintendent of Schools (2024) PERB Decision
No. 2934, p. 16.) Ultimately, the parties must persuade one another of their positions,
and the neutral factfinder simply provides an outside perspective to assist the parties
to possibly come to an agreement over matters within the scope of representation.
(Government Code section 3548; City of Oakland (2018) PERB Order No. Ad-462-M,
p. 4; County of Ventura (2018) PERB Order No. Ad-461-M, p. 5.) Both parties to the
factfinding process are statutorily obligated to participate in this process in good faith.
(Regents of the University of California, supra, p. 6; San Bernardino County
Superintendent of Schools, supra, p. 16.)
Reduction in Hours of the LMTAs/LMAs at the Six Remaining School Library Sites
The District finds itself in an ongoing fiscal dilemma of having to face the
continuing reality of significant declining student enrollment from over a decade, into
the 2026-2027 school year, and beyond (to the 2033-2034 school year). The District
has instituted a fiscal stabilization plan in order to provide stability for the District given
14

the loss of federal and state pandemic relief funds that were expiring and in order to
provide fiscal stability for the District. It has made reductions in other areas besides
library services to achieve this goal.
While the District has decided to eliminate other positions in other
classifications, it has decided instead to reduce the hours of LMTAs/LMAs in order
that the District may provide the appropriate level of library media services to its
students at its individual school library sites. The District measured the duties of its
LMTAs/LMAs based upon the present need of the individual classes which
LMTAs/LMAs host and the preparation time associated with hosting these individual
classes; the hosting of lunch/recess periods for students; and the other duties within
the LMTA/LMA job descriptions not related to the hosting of individual classes which
were to be performed on Thursdays. This focused targeting of LMTA/LMA duties was
reasonable and logical to the primary mission of the District’s education of its students.
The numbers of reduced hours per week based upon these core duties fall closer to
the numbers of reduced hours per week set forth in the District’s proposals than
CSEA’s proposals.
CSEA asserts that some of the hourly reductions of LMTAs/LMAs are too
severe and will lead to future recruitment and retention issues and that the District
possesses an adequate amount of unrestricted cash reserves which provide the
District with the ability to absorb the cost of a smaller reduction in hours similar to
CSEA’s proposal. This argument carries some weight, especially as to the 37 percent
reduction in hours proposed upon the LMTA/LMA employed at Garfield School, and
the Chair agrees that such a reduction in hours to that position will cause
15

recruitment/retention problems in the future. However, as the decline of student
enrollment has not been forecasted to reverse nor even plateau, CSEA’s argument
ultimately loses its force. Unfortunately for both the District and CSEA, the decline of
student enrollment will continue. As such, it is in the interests and welfare of the
public and the financial ability of the public school employer that the hourly reductions
in the LMTAs/LMAs’ workweek as proposed by the District be accepted, with a
modification as to implementation of the effective date of the reduction in hours being
postponed to the beginning of the upcoming 2026-2027 school year.
Recommendation(s) for Settlement: Pursuant to Government Code
section 3548.2, subdivision (b)(3), the Chair recommends that the District’s proposal
as to the reduction in hours of the LMTAs/LMAs as to the six remaining individual
library sites, including its augmented health benefits proposal, be accepted by the
parties. The effective date of the reduction of hours, however, should start at the
beginning of the 2026-2027 school year as the LMTAs/LMAs have already worked the
hours scheduled for them in the 2025-2026 school year.
In addition to such recommendation, it is also recommended that by the end of
fall semester of the 2026-2027 school year, that the District conduct an evaluation as
to the adequacy of the allotment of the reduced weekly hours of the LMTAs/LMAs as
to the six remaining school library sites in order to determine whether the
LMTAs/LMAs are able to complete the duties set forth in their job descriptions within
the reduced allotment of weekly hours. Such evaluation shall include seeking input
from CSEA and the unit employee affected by the weekly reduction in hours.
16

CONCLUSION
The Chair is sincerely hopeful that these recommendations will assist the
parti1as in their negotiations going forward and which eventually will result in the
parties coming to a resolution of this matter.

DISSENT OF EMPLOYEE ORGANIZATION PANEL MEMBER
I respectfully dissent from the Chair's recommendation that the District's proposal regarding the
reduction of hours for the remaining Library Media Technical Associate (“LMTA”) and Library
Media Assistant (“LMA”) positions be adopted.
The record establishes that the District faces legitimate fiscal challenges arising from declining
enrollment and the expiration of one-time funding sources. However, the evidence does not
demonstrate that the magnitude of the proposed reductions is necessary or that the District's
staffing analysis fully accounts for the scope of duties performed by LMTAs and LMAs.
The District's rationale is based primarily upon scheduled student contact time, associated
preparation periods, and designated work periods. Yet the job descriptions for both
classifications include numerous responsibilities that are not directly tied to classroom
scheduling, including collection maintenance, circulation management, literacy support,
assistance to students and staff, supervision of volunteers, development of library programming,
and other operational functions essential to the effective operation of school libraries. The record
does not persuasively establish that these duties can be adequately performed within the
substantially reduced hours proposed by the District.
Moreover, the proposed reductions would have a significant adverse impact on affected
employees, particularly at Garfield School where the reductions are especially severe. The Chair
expressly recognizes the likelihood that at least some of these reductions may create recruitment
and retention concerns. This consideration weighs against adopting the District's proposal in its
entirety.
Further evidence demonstrates that CSEA's final proposal would still produce meaningful and
ongoing cost savings while reducing the adverse effects on bargaining unit employees and
preserving a greater level of library services for students. In light of the District's acknowledged
reserve levels and the relatively limited fiscal difference between the parties' positions, a less
drastic reduction in hours better balances the District's financial interests with the interests of
employees and the educational needs of the District's students.
For these reasons, I would reject the District's proposed reductions and recommend adoption of a
modified staffing plan more closely aligned with CSEA's final proposal, together with a
subsequent evaluation of workload and service delivery during the 2026-2027 school year.
Accordingly, I dissent.
Dated: June 2, 2026
Nathan Jennings, Senior Labor Relations Representative
CSEA Panel Member

FACTFINDING PROCEEDINGS
PURSUANT TO THE MEYERS-MILIAS-BROWN ACT

PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND
On September 17, 2025, the Redding Independent Employees Organization
(RIEO) filed two factfinding requests with the Public Employment Relations Board
(PERB or Board) pursuant to the Meyers-Milias-Brown Act1 (MMBA) regarding its
successor agreement negotiations in its Supervisory/Confidential Unit (PERB Case
No. SA-IM-255-M) and its Clerical, Technical and Professional (CTP) Unit (PERB
Case No. SA-IM-256-M) with the City of Redding (City).
On September 19, 2025, PERB approved the factfinding requests for a
factfinding proceeding to be conducted.2 On February 25, 2026, RIEO notified PERB
as to its factfinding panel member. On February 26, 2026, the City notified PERB as
to its selection of a factfinding panel member and the parties’ selection of the
undersigned neutral factfinder as the factfinding panel chair (Chair). On February 27,
2026, PERB notified the undersigned factfinder that he had been selected as the
Chair of the factfinding panel.
On March 13, 2026, the Chair held an organizational meeting where the Chair
and the parties discussed: the agenda of the factfinding proceeding, an early
exchange of presentations, the factfinding proceeding dates, and the issuance date of
the factfinding report and recommendations for settlement (factfinding report). The

FINDINGS OF FACT
Prior Memorandum of Understanding
RIEO bargaining unit employees provide essential services to the residents of
Redding, including public works, community services, development and general
government functions.6 The prior MOU between RIEO and the City for both the CTP
Unit and Supervisory/Confidential Unit had a term of July 20, 2022 to July 19, 2025.
According to the report to the City Council, the “Terms and Wages” of the agreement
was:
6 The City has approximately 11-12 bargaining units.
5

“● 3-year contract, effective through July 19, 2025.
“● An approximate 8 percent average overall wage increase, effective
July 24, 2022. Wage increases vary by classification from 3 percent
to 23.75 percent[.]
“● A 5 percent general wage increase, effective July 23, 2023.
“● A 5 percent general wage increase, effective July 21, 2024.”
While RIEO acknowledged that the prior MOU gave large wage/salary
increases to its bargaining unit employees, it contended that these increases only
brought RIEO unit employees within parity of other regional governmental agencies.
Remaining Disputed Proposals
While the parties have reached tentative agreement on many terms while
attempting to negotiate successor contracts for both bargaining units,7 the remaining
three disputes generally center on the issue of the ability of the public agency to pay
for the ongoing increases to RIEO’s bargaining unit employees’ salaries.
A. General Salary Increase of 2 Percent
RIEO last salary proposal to the City was passed during post impasse
proceedings—that the City provide a 2 percent general salary increase to all RIEO
bargaining unit employees. The agreed cost of the proposal to the City’s general fund
was $350,759 a year.8 Because of the City’s concern as to its financial inability to pay

1. City’s Financial Outlook and the City’s Policy regarding maintaining
Adequate Cash Reserves
The City passed a resolution in 1992 entitled, “Establishment of Long-Range
Financial Plans and Unreserved Cash Balance,” which is commonly referred to as City
Council Policy 412. City Council Policy 412 was enacted in order for the City to have
a fiscally responsible policy which ensured that the City had financial stability and was
able to continue providing City services for a limited period of time, especially in times
of emergency, and not become insolvent. City Council Policy 412 provides in
pertinent part:
“It is the policy of the City Council of the City of Redding:
“1. To prepare long-range financial plans for each of the City’s
major funds and update those plans at least biennially.
“2. To maintain at a minimum an estimated ten percent[9] of
projected expenditures unreserved cash balance at year end
throughout the long-range financial plan.
“[ . . . ]
believed the cost to the City’s general fund was the relevant issue in determining the
City’s ability to pay. The City strenuously argued that it was prohibited by case law
from utilizing enterprise funds earmarked for specific purposes to pay for general fund
allocation(s). For the most part, RIEO did not counter the City’s assertion.
9 The Government Finance Officers Association (GFOA) recommends as a best
practice that governmental agencies maintain an unrestricted cash fund balance in the
general fund as to no less than 60 days or two months of operating expenditures,
which is the equivalent of maintaining an unreserved cash balance of 17 percent of
the entity’s projected expenditures by the end of the fiscal year. It should be noted
that City Council Policy 412 falls short of GFOA’s best practice.
7

“4. A requested appropriation that would cause the estimated end
of year cash reserve in any year of the long-range financial
plan to drop below ten percent needs to be submitted with a
plan to insure the fiscal stability of major fund’s financial
position. . . .”
The City stated that the 10 percent minimum cash reserves allowed the City to
meet its operating expenditures for approximately one month in a time of emergency.
If all of the City’s cash reserves were spent, the City would be considered insolvent.
a. June 17, 2025 Adopted Biennial Budget
On June 17, 2025, the City adopted its biennial budget for fiscal years ending
June 30, 2026 and June 30, 2027. The adopted budget expressly stated that “all
funds should maintain a 10 percent of annual expenditures reserve, . . .” The adopted
budget showed that the City began fiscal year 2025/2026 with general fund reserves
below the 10 percent level of required cash reserves, but the City believed it would be
able to increase its reserves over the fiscal year to rise above the 10 percent level
(10.7 percent ). The budget document stated regarding “Economic Conditions and
Revenue Constraints”:
“Over the past two years, the regional economy has stalled - local
consumer purchases are down and not meeting projections as inflation
increased and online purchases increased, which in turn redirected tax
allocations to other locations. Thereby, the City experienced significant
underperformance in sales tax revenue, the single largest contributor to
the General Fund. The shortfall— approximately $2.9 million that
compounds prior biennial budget shortfall of more than $3 million —
combined with new regulatory requirements, increased personnel, risk
management, and maintenance costs, and inflation-driven increases in
materials, fuel, and contract costs; collectively, has placed a heavy strain
on departmental budgets. Operational overruns, particularly in
maintenance and public safety, became unavoidable due to price
volatility and supply chain issues.
8

“These revenue declines and economic uncertainties necessitated
conservative forecasting for this budget. The City’s long-term financial
plan assumes modest tax growth, yet reserves have been meaningfully
depleted. Staff will rigorously continue to monitor trends and recommend
adjustments as appropriate.”
Regarding “Right-sizing and Position Reductions,” the budget document
provided:
“To bring expenditures in line with declining revenues, the proposed
budget eliminates several positions through attrition. These include eight
sworn police officer positions, a Fire Marshal, a Senior Planner, two
Assistant City Clerk positions, and other staff across various
departments. The workforce reductions were carefully selected to
minimize service disruption while aligning staffing levels with sustainable
revenue projections.
“Additionally, operations and maintenance budgets have been reduced
by more than five percent across most departments. While necessary,
these cuts carry long-term risks. If revenues do not rebound, aging
infrastructure and deferred maintenance will lead to increased costs
and/or service degradation in the next few years.”
According to the adopted budget for fiscal year 2025/2026, the City received its
revenue for its general fund expenditures primarily from sales tax (28.4 percent of
general fund revenue), property tax (27.7 percent of general fund revenue), and the
transient occupancy tax (7 percent of general fund revenue). The revenue
assumptions by the City were that its sales tax revenue would increase by 2 percent
from the previous fiscal year and property tax would increase by 3 percent from the
previous fiscal year. In recent years for the City, sales tax revenue has been
considered to be the most volatile sources of revenue, while property tax revenue has
been considered to be the most reliable source of revenue.
9

b. November 18, 2025 Quarterly Financial Report to the
City Council
On or about November 18, 2025, City Finance Director Greg Robinett
(Robinett) submitted to the City Council the General Fund Quarterly Report for the
quarter ending September 30, 2025. The total general fund revenue received by the
City up to September 30, 2025 was $19,350,759 or 15 percent below the cash flow
projection. The total general fund of expenditures spent by the City was $30,952,404,
which was 2.9 percent above the projected revenue. The general fund cash balance
was down to 3.1 percent. Robinett did not recommend any potential modifications to
the fiscal year 2025/2026 adopted budget, but stated that the City needed to consider
potential modifications at the mid-fiscal year budget update, which ended on
December 31, 2025. Robinett noted that the sales tax revenue had underperformed in
comparison with the City’s growth assumptions
c. February 3, 2026 Biennial Budget Revenue Discussion
Robinett prepared a report for the City Council Meeting on February 3, 2026,
entitled, “Biennial Budget Revenue Discussion” for fiscal year 2025/2026 and fiscal
year 2026/2027. As a result of the report, the City made changes to its assumptions
for revenue projections so that it reduced the amount that the City expected to receive
in sales tax, transit occupancy taxes, and cannabis tax.
d. March 17, 2026 Mid-Fiscal Year Update before the City Council
Robinette prepared a report for the City Council Meeting on March 17, 2026,
entitled, “Mid-Year Budget Review and Adoption of the Associated Resolution.”
Robinett noted in the report that as of December 31, 2025, the total general fund
revenue was $42,912,180 or 5.43 percent below cash flow projection and the total
10

general fund expenditures were $60,930,497, which was slightly above (0.82 percent)
its cash flow estimate. In short, at the mid-fiscal year point in the budget, the City was
spending much more than it was bringing in.
e. Austerity Measures taken by the City in light of its Revenue
Shortfall
In light of the City’s revenue shortfall in the fiscal year 2025/2026 budget, the
City implemented the following austerity measures across all City departments to
reduce the level of expenditures: (1) freezing all hiring, except for mission-critical
positions; (2) freezing all overtime work, except for mission-critical positions; and
(3) freezing all expenditures, except for mission-critical positions. In addition, the City
adopted a ten-year budgetary plan reflecting adjustments to its revenue projections,
ordered staff to continuously assess and evaluate opportunities as to how to save
funds and make the workplace more efficient, and contracted with a third party to
conduct a citywide efficiency study.
2. Beacon Economics Opinion as to the Future Revenue of the City
Beacon Economics (Beacon) is an independent research and consulting firm
dedicated to providing objectively based economic analysis. Beacon was retained by
RIEO to provide an opinion as to whether the City had the ability to pay for the three
disputed proposals of RIEO. After analyzing a number of factors such as employment
growth, the labor force, the unemployment rate, taxable sales, active local investment,
home prices, improved home sale activity, increased revenue from the transient
occupancy tax over time, and other factors, Beacon concluded that the City could pay
for the proposals. Beacon forecasted that it expected total tax revenues for the City to
grow 2 to 3 percent through fiscal year 2027/2028.
11

Beacon offered no opinion as to whether its forecast as to the City’s revenues
could pay for all of the City’s expenditures as expenditures were a policy choice to be
made by the City.
3. Consumer Price Index
The West Region’s Consumer Price Index (CPI), which includes Redding,
California, rose 3.1 percent for the twelve months ending in March 2026. RIEO claims
that its 2 percent general salary increase proposal was modest when compared to the
CPI for the region. The City contends that the CPI increase of 3.1 percent is
outweighed by the City’s inability to pay for such an increase in light of its
expenditures outweighing its revenues and its compromised 10 percent cash reserve
level.
4. General Salary Increases provided by other Regional MMBA Public
Agencies
RIEO contends that while the City of Redding helped RIEO bargaining unit
employees gain parity with other regional and similarly situated represented
governmental MMBA employees in its prior MOU, the RIEO bargaining unit employees
will soon fall behind these same MMBA regional governmental employers based upon
general salary increases given by these same regional governmental employers. The
City of Chico10 provided general employees with a 4.5 percent general salary increase
effective March 8, 2026, and the County of Shasta provided its supervisory employees
with a 2 percent general salary increase effective March 8, 2026, and its general

2026 to December 31, 2027, Article 5.1. G. Official notice is taken of this document
without an objection from either party.
12

employees with a 2 percent general salary increase effective January or
February 2026.11
B. Administrative Clerk Reclassification Proposal
On July 23, 2025, the parties tentatively agreed to an Administrative Clerk
Reclassification proposal. The proposal, in effect, consolidated two series
classifications (Clerk I/II/III and Administrative Assistant I/II) into a newly created
Administrative Clerk I/II/III series classification. In addition, the proposal removed the
minimum requirement of supervisory experience to apply for the Executive
Assistant I/II series classification and renamed the Officer Services Supervisor
classification to an Office Services Manager classification.
On February 19, 2026, the City informed RIEO that it rescinded this tentative
agreement due to the changed circumstances of the City’s overall fiscal concerns
regarding the impact of this proposal on the City’s general fund.
RIEO argued that the factfinding panel should recommend the Administrative
Clerk Reclassification proposal as the City should honor its tentative agreements with
RIEO.12

C. Customer Service Representative Reclassification Proposal
On July 23, 2025, the parties tentatively agreed to a Customer Service
Representative Reclassification proposal. The proposal, in effect, incorporated the
Scale House Attendant I/II/III series classification into a proposed expanded Customer
Service Representative I/II series classification.13 The incumbent Scale House
Attendant I/II/III employees were to be placed in the Customer Service
Representative I classification and the incumbent Customer Service Representative
employees would be placed in the Customer Service Representative II classification.
In addition, this proposal created a Utility Billing Specialist classification which
contained a wage increase of 5 percent above the Customer Service Representative
wage range.
On February 19, 2026, the City informed RIEO that it rescinded this tentative
agreement due to the changed circumstances as to the City’s overall fiscal concerns
and concerns about pending rate increases and the perception that the City is raising
its utility rates to fund wage increases.
RIEO argued that the factfinding panel should recommend the Customer
Service Representative Reclassification proposal as the City should honor its
agreements with RIEO.
APPLICATION OF STATUTORY CRITERIA and RECOMMENDATIONS
Unlike interest arbitration, where a third-party neutral sets the terms of a
new agreement, a third-party neutral in an MMBA factfinding report simply provides
13 Prior to this proposed expanded Customer Service Representative I/II series
classification, the Customer Service Representative classification only included a
singular Customer Service Representative classification rather than a series.
14

recommendation(s) as to terms for settlement, which shall be advisory only.
(Gov. Code, § 3505.5, subd. (a).) In essence, the impasse resolution procedure,
which includes the factfinding process, is a continuation of the collective bargaining
process. (Regents of the University of California (2026) PERB Decision No. 3010-H,
p. 5; San Bernardino County Superintendent of Schools (2024) PERB Decision
No. 2934, p. 16.) Ultimately, the parties must persuade one another of their positions,
and the neutral factfinder simply provides an outside perspective to assist the parties
possibly to come to an agreement over matters within the scope of representation.
(City of Oakland (2018) PERB Order No. Ad-462-M, p. 4; County of Ventura (2018)
PERB Order No. Ad-461-M, p. 5.) Both parties to the factfinding process are
statutorily obligated to participate in this process in good faith. (Regents of the
University of California, supra, p. 6; San Bernardino County Superintendent of
Schools, supra, p. 16.)
After carefully considering the record as a whole, the findings of fact, and the
statutory criteria in Government Code section 3505.4, subdivision (d), the Chair
applies the most pertinent statutory criteria to those findings of fact, and recommends
the following by issue:
General Salary Increase of 2 Percent
It is clear that the City is experiencing a revenue shortfall of a magnitude where
its expenditures exceed its revenues, and it needs to take action to maintain a
10 percent cash reserve so that it does not become insolvent. In reality, the proposal
of the 2 percent salary increase will not only cost the City’s general fund $350,759 a
year, but the cost will multiply as it will most likely include other bargaining units who
15

attempt to bargain for similar increases with the City. While RIEO argues that the
region’s CPI increase and increases provided by other similar regional MMBA public
agencies to general/supervisory employees weigh toward granting a 2 percent salary
increase, RIEO has not established that these factors outweigh the interests and
welfare of the public in having a more financially stable City government and that the
City is financially unable to pay for such a salary increase during a time when the
City’s expenditures outpace its revenue and the general fund cash reserves fall below
10 percent.
Recommendation(s) for settlement: Pursuant to Government Code section 3505.4,
subdivision (d)(4), the Chair recommends that the general salary of RIEO bargaining
unit employees remain status quo.
Reclassification Proposals (Administrative Clerk and Customer Service
Representative)
The two reclassification proposals, the Administrative Clerk Reclassification and
Customer Service Representative Reclassification proposals, will be evaluated
together. The Customer Service Representative Reclassification proposal carries a
greater cost ($85,782) than the Administrative Clerk Reclassification proposal
($26,969). Admittedly, the City faces the same ongoing cost issues regarding these
proposals as it did with the general salary increase proposal, except to a lesser extent,
especially as such proposals may not be the subject to similar demands by other
bargaining units who are negotiating with the City.
Just as the City has engaged in austerity measures in examining itself to create
efficiencies and savings for the City, these proposals should likewise be evaluated.
The Customer Service Representative Reclassification proposal will reduce the
16

number of examinations the City will have to conduct by having the Scale House
Attendant I/II/III series classification incorporated into the Customer Service
Representative I/II classification. This efficiency should be able to save the City,
especially the personnel department, the time and expense of conducting duplicative
examinations. On the other hand, the Customer Service Representative
Reclassification proposal also included the creation of a new classification, the Utility
Billing Specialist, which would create an inefficiency by increasing the number of
examinations which the personnel department would need to conduct, instead of
folding those positions into an existing City classification. As such, it does not seem
that this proposal creates any efficiencies along with its cost, and therefore the cost to
the City in the time of the City’s financial inability to pay militate toward this proposal
as remaining status quo.
On the other hand, the Administrative Clerk Reclassification proposal
consolidates two separate classifications (the Clerk I/II/III series classification and the
Administrative Assistant I/II series classification) into one new series classification.
Such a consolidation would eventually create an efficiency to the City by eliminating a
duplicative examination process, and reduce the time and expense expended by the
City’s personnel department. This efficiency, and the reduced time and savings that
come from this proposal, should be considered by the City when evaluating the cost of
the proposal—especially as the cost of the Administrative Clerk Reclassification
proposal is relatively minimal at $26,969 a year. In addition, if this reclassification
proposal was implemented on a deferred basis, the City may be able to implement it
after its austerity measures have been able to increase the general fund cash reserve
17

minimum to 10 percent and reverse the current problem where expenditures are
exceeding revenues.
Recommendation(s) for settlement: Pursuant to Government Code section 3505.4,
subdivision (d)(4), the Chair recommends the parties remain status quo as to the
Customer Service Representative Reclassification proposal and that the parties
accept the Administrative Clerk Reclassification proposal with a deferred
implementation date in order to defer the cost of the implementation of the proposal.
18

CONCLUSION
The Chair is sincerely hopeful that these recommendations will assist the
parties in their negotiations going forward and which eventually will result in the
parties coming to a resolution of this matter.

DISTRICT AND ASSOCIATION DESCRIPTIONS
The Little Lake City School District (District or Management) is a suburban elementary school
district located in the southeastern portion of Los Angeles County. The District lies within the
municipalities of Santa Fe Springs, Norwalk, and Downey. The nine schools, seven elementary
and two middle, serve a diverse student population of 3,396. The ethnic distribution of the
student body is approximately 90% Hispanic, 2.8% White/non-Hispanic, 1.4% African-
American, and approximately 6% other. English learners account for 8.1% of the student
population, and 66.5% of English learners identify their primary language as Spanish.
Approximately 79% of students districtwide qualify for free/reduced lunch. All nine schools
receive federal Title I, and state Local Control Funds (including supplemental and concentration
funds for English learners, socioeconomically disadvantaged, and foster students). The District
offers a full-day transitional kindergarten and kindergarten program at all seven elementary sites.
An emphasis on learning, collaboration, and results is reflected in many of the practices at all
sites.
Little Lake Education Association (LLEA or Union) was established in December 1976. It is the
union representing 199 members, including general education and special education classroom
teachers, teachers on special assignment (TOSAs), one school nurse, one speech language
pathologist, and one adapted PE teacher.
LLEA operates as a local union chapter affiliated with the California Teachers Association
(CTA) and the National Education Association (NEA). Through these affiliations, the
association participates in statewide efforts to advocate for public education, educators, and
students.
HISTORY OF NEGOTIATIONS
The parties “sunshined” their respective proposals to the public on May 7, 2025 and May , and
met for four sessions from September 2025 through October 2025. PERB certified an impasse
and a mediator from the State Medication and Conciliation Service was assigned. The parties
had five mediation sessions from January 14 through February 20, 2026. The mediator certified
the parties to fact finding on February 23, 2026.
FACTFINDING CRITERIA
Pursuant to California Government Code Section 3548.2, the panel has considered and been
guided by the following statutory criteria:
1. State and federal laws that are applicable to the Employer.
2. Stipulations of the parties.
3. The interests and welfare of the public and the financial ability of the public
schools.
4. Comparison of the wages, hours, and conditions of employment of the employees
involved in the fact-finding proceeding with the wages, hours, and conditions of
2

employment of other employees performing similar services and with other
employees generally in public school employment in comparable communities.
5. The Consumer Price Index for goods and services, commonly known as the cost of
living.
6. The overall compensation presently received by the employees, including direct
wage compensation, vacations, holidays, and other excused time, insurance and
pensions, medical and hospitalization benefits, the continuity and stability of
employment, and all other benefits received.
7. Such other facts not confined to those specified in paragraphs 1 through 6,
inclusive, which are normally and traditionally taken into consideration in making
such findings and recommendations.
ISSUES BEFORE THE PANEL
There are five Articles before the Panel:
• Article XII – Class Size
• Article XIX – Hours of Employment
• Article XVII– Miscellaneous
• Article XX – Compensation
• Article XXI – Health and Welfare Benefits
Chair’s note: The parties have reached verbal consensus on some of the provisions under some
of these Articles. The Chair will focus the attention on the outstanding provisions presented at
the Hearing and will assume the parties will incorporate those verbal agreements within the
appropriate Articles when agreement on the entire collective bargaining agreement is reached.
The Chair’s Findings and Recommendations
The parties find themselves in a dilemma around Health and Welfare benefits. For
approximately the past 20 years, the District and the Association have entered into a series of
agreements that used one-time funding to provide additional employer contributions to the
District cap contributions established in the parties Collective Bargaining Agreement (“CBA”).
Those negotiated additional contributions provided full benefit coverages with no out-of-pocket
monthly employee contributions. Unfortunately, the benefit “caps” remained in the contract and
were not adjusted upwards as benefit costs increased. This plan year, beginning January 1, 2026,
the District chose to enforce the caps contained within the CBA without supplementing the costs
with any kind of funding, one-time or ongoing, and employees found themselves from paying $0
out-of-pocket to in some cases paying almost $1,400 per month (Kaiser with family option).
This decision to cease relying on one-time funding to ignore addressing the real benefit cap in
the CBA has soured the relationship and effects all aspects of this reopened negotiations. The
3

Chair’s recommendations on all Articles will center around establishing permanent, on-going
funding to Health and Welfare Benefits and cease the use of one-time funding for this purpose.
After a review of the facts and arguments presented by both parties, the Chair recommends the
following for each of the Articles before the panel:
Term (Combination of Article I and Article V)
The Parties have been negotiating for eleven months and the tone of bargaining has turned
contentious. Although they reached impasse on the last year, 2025-2026, of a three year
agreement, the Chair believes the parties would benefit from being away from the bargaining
table instead of immediately reopening the successor year, 2026-2027. The Chair is firm in his
belief that an agreement is preferable to a job action and a “locked-down” contract through 2026-
2027 would benefit both sides. It will also give clear predictability for personal budgets for the
union members and for District budget planning for 2026-27
Recommendation 1: Term – The Chair recommends the parties close 2025-2026 and
enter into a 3 year Agreement from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2029. All Articles
would be closed for 2026-2027 and 2027-2028 will have reopeners on all Compensation
(Articles XX and XI) with three additional Articles per side. Additionally, for 2027-
2028, each party could propose a new Article on Special Education. Reopeners for 2028-
2029 will be all Compensation (Articles XX and XI) with three additional Articles per
side.
Article XII – Class Size
From the materials provided by each side and the Union’s presentation, it appears to the Chair
that the District has not staffed class sizes to the levels contained the CBA. The District
estimates that between retirements and possible reductions in force (RIFs) there is a possibility
that nine unit members will not be replaced in 2026-2027, thereby effecting class sizes as well as
relieving the budget commitment of almost $1 million. This would be a key source of ongoing
funding.
The District has proposed these additional increases to class size for 2026-2027 and 2027-2028:
2026-2027
• TK-3 increase average class size to 27:1, with Kindergarten classes capped at 27
• 4-6 staffing ratios at 1:33
• 7-8 Staffing ratios at 1:30
2026-2027
• TK-3 increase average class size to 27:1, with Kindergarten classes capped at 27
• 4-6 staffing ratios at 1:33
• 7-8 Staffing ratios at 1:30

From the data, the Chair believes the District has not staffed to the limits within this Article but
does agree that raising and staffing to the limits would result in fewer staff generating more
available ongoing funding. The proposed TK-3 numbers would increase the average by 3
immediately, which may be too large in increase in one year.
Recommendation 2: Class Size - The Chair recommends the following adjustments:

Article XXI – Health and Welfare Benefits
Health Benefit premium are calculated for the calendar year, January 1 through December 31,
which will span two fiscal years. Out of pocket employee contributions are paid tenthly, but the
District must pay the premiums twelfthly. This calculation often confuses people. The Chair
will use the annual premium (which again is the calendar year and spans two fiscal years) for his
recommendation.
The Chair’s recommendation must attempt to address ongoing funding for Health and Welfare
benefits while keeping in mind the District’s budget. Also, the days of low class size and fully
provided benefits with no out of pocket may be over for the foreseeable future with the
forecasted state funding. Using the approximate million dollars generated from the decrease in
staff to provide on-going funding, the Chair makes the following recommendation.
Recommendation 3: Health and Welfare Benefits
New language in the CBA will have the District funding the Blue Shield Access Plus at
85% of premium at all tiers (ee, ee+1, ee+2 or more) with the employee paying 15% out-
of-pocket. The amount of 85% of Blue Shield Access Plus will be the “cap” spent on
every other plan at all tiers. Should the choice of plans change, the parties will reach
agreement on a new base plan as nearest to cost as Blue Shield Access Plus.
Article XX – Compensation (Salary)
Recognizing the priority of funding Health and Welfare, neither side proposed any ongoing
adjustment to the schedule.
5

Both side acknowledge the need for recruiting and retaining Speech and Language Pathologists
(SLP), both sides exchanged proposals for a new schedule to help recruit and retain SLPs to
eliminate the more expensive option of contracting out. The Chair recommends the District’s
position for a new Speech and Language Pathologist Salary Schedule.
Two other items are in this category of Compensation. It appears that the parties have a mutual
interest in compensating 5th grade teachers attending Science Camp with a one-time $500
stipend. It also appears that the parties have a mutual interest in compensating SDC

levels shall be paid an annual stipend of $1,000 and moderate/severe elementary teachers

• Adopt Speech and Language Pathologist Salary Schedule as proposed by the
District (Attachment #1)
• $500 stipend for 5th grade teachers attending Science Camp
• $1000 annual stipend for SDC mild/moderate elementary teachers assigned to a
combination classroom of three or more grade levels
• $1000 annual stipend for moderate/severe elementary teachers assigned to a
combination classroom of four or more grade levels
Article XIX – Hours of Employment
Again, there may be some consensus regarding some provisions in this section, but the
outstanding issue seemed to be completing annual training during the first week of school. The
District wishes that the teachers complete that annual training during one of the minimum days
of that first week and the Association proposes it not be done during preparation time. It seems
the parties agree to increase the first week of school from 3 minimum days to as many as 5
minimum days. It seems obvious to the Chair that this required training be completed sometime
during that first week and the District proposal does not seem to be onerous, especially if the first
week of minimum days have increased.
Recommendation 5: Hours
Teachers to complete the required annual training during the first week of school and
the site administrator be charged with managing the timing of that training.
Article XVII – Miscellaneous
Candidly, the Chair was somewhat at a loss with this seemingly catch-all Article, appropriately
named “Miscellaneous”. There were over a dozen and a half seemingly unrelated items in this
that, frankly seem too much of a stretch of effort to resolve each one. A number of these issues
6

were new and related to Special Education and seemed unrelated to other items in this Article.
The Chair will leave it to the parties to resolve this category of “Miscellaneous” as much better
prepared to understand each of the nuances and discussions that preceded the impasse.
However, since a number of these provisions do seem to revolve around Special Education, the
Chair feels it appropriate to address how the parties can move forward on items regarding
Special Education. Included in the material the Association presented at the Hearing, was a
March 5, 2005 document titled, “Special Education Study” completed by Bridge 2 Inclusive
Practices. This over 100 page document is a study of the Little Lake City School District with,
the Chair assumes, an overall assessment of current services and recommendations regarding its
Special Ed program.
Several of the proposed changes under this “Miscellaneous” Article likely originated from this
study. The Chair is not an expert in Special Education and does not feel confident making
recommendations regarding specific programs or the personnel who provide these services to
students. However, the Chair does have knowledge of best practices in labor-management
collaboration to address such issues.
The Chair strongly believes that a joint committee, task force, or recommending body composed
of experienced district practitioners and managers would be best equipped to develop informed
recommendations based on this study. Engaging the individuals most directly affected by
potential changes—alongside program managers—in a collaborative process is far more likely to
result in meaningful and positive outcomes than proposals exchanged solely across the
negotiations table. Additionally, the Chair believes the parties would benefit from moving away
from confrontational negotiations to a process of dialogue and problem solving. The parties
could place any recommendations in a new Article of the CBA titled “Special Education” or
embed them within existing Articles of the CBA (not “Miscellaneous”).
Recommendation 6: Miscellaneous
The Chair recommends the formation of a Special Education Task Force with the
following:
• An equal number of participants from the Association and the Administration
• Joint co-chairs
• The charge of this Task Force is to implementing recommendations from the
expert report and, with fidelity, address concerns raised within district programs
• Use consensus decision-making after being trained in Interest Based Problem
Solving.

Dissenting In Part Report of Panel Member Su
PERB CASE NO: LA-IM-4206-E
Little Lake City School District and Little Lake Education Association
Su, Panel Member for the union, dissenting in part:
Health and Welfare Benefits
Although I agree that the main item at issue between the parties is health benefits, the supposed use of
one-time funds to provide employer contributions above the 2015 cap is an example of a clear lack of
the District prioritizing employee compensation in the form of health benefits which is an expense that
is reasonably predictable year-over-year and a benefit necessary to attract and retain qualified
employees. The Union’s analysis of the LLCSD’s finances demonstrates how LLCSD can prioritize
employee educator health and welfare benefits in its budget. LLCSD has an increasing trend of
spending more each year on outside contractors for positions that should be filled by employees who
are in the best position to meet the needs of students. Adjusting this pattern and actually budgeting
increases to revenue that have already been articulated by the Governor’s January State Budget
Proposal will provide sufficient funding to meet LLEAs health benefits demands without the need to
increase class sizes in 2026-27. The District should have sufficient time to convert contracted positions
in the 2026-27 school year to employees, and given the 15 layoff notices already issued, the District
may already have the staff to fill those positions.
I commend the chair’s efforts in recommending the Blue Shield Access Plus plan as the basis of an
ongoing premium sharing arrangement. However, 85%/15% is too high an out of pocket premium
contribution per month (employee $165, $ employee + 1 $330, family $430; Kaiser employee $227, $
employee + 1 $498, family $589) and I would suggest a 90%/10% split as a more reasonable
compromise moving down from 100% paid coverage that has been the standard in the district for
decades. This would align them with comparable districts. At the high out-of-pocket premiums LLEA
educators are currently paying for Blue Shield Access Plus (employee $410, employee + 1 $819,
family $1,065), LLCSD is ranked lower than all neighboring districts for healthcare contributions.
High out-of-pocket healthcare premiums coupled with a zero salary increase in 2025-26, the District
can expect to lose educators to districts with better compensation.
I concur that the implementation of whatever the parties agree to in the way of health benefits should
be ongoing and retroactive to January 2026, to provide some relief for the very extreme out-of-pocket
costs educators are enduring now.
Compensation
Although the LLCSD’s certificated salary compensation ranks poorly, the union chose, for 2025-26 to
prioritize fully paid health benefits, therefore I concur with the chair’s recommendation for no change
in the salary schedule for 2025-26. In addition, the remaining compensation recommendations are also
appropriate.
Class Size
It is important to note that class size was not even an issue on the table for most of the pre-impasse
negotiations and was a late sunshine by the District and only proposed as part of a package deal that
1

the Union rejected. Therefore, they have had little actual discussion about how these changes would
impact educator working conditions, student learning conditions, and the estimated value of the
savings that the District would achieve by worsening those conditions.
I concur with the chair that the District should certainly staff to the class size ratios and caps that are
already in the CBA before demanding higher class sizes. I also agree that with the current layoffs and
natural attrition, the District will save more than $1 million dollars in 2026-27 which should absolutely
be used to support the costs of employee health benefits moving forward.
As a practical matter, it is unlikely that the District would be able to implement any further changes to
class size in the 2026-27 year unless there is an unexpected exodus of teachers before the start of next
year as they have indicated that the current layoffs and anticipated retirements would only allow them
to staff to the current CBA. Therefore, there is no point in agreeing to higher class sizes for 2026-27
and it is not appropriate to tie up the agreement beyond 2026-27 (see comments on Term below).
Hours of Employment
I concur that the parties had some conceptual agreement on having minimum days the first week of
instruction for 2026-27. I would like to expand on the chair’s recommendation to clarify that this
online training be done post student dismissal on the two days that are already allotted to site
administrator discretion.
Term
The year at impasse is 2025-26 and given how late we are in the academic year, a two year term, 2025-
27 is reasonable. The Association intends to negotiate a successor agreement after that and should be
afforded the right to do so since 2026-27 would be the year for a successor agreement given the term
of the current CBA.
Miscellaneous
The chair has recommended the formation of a Special Education Task Force ostensibly to implement
the recommendations from the expert report which I concur that said special education report
recommendations should be implemented. Until such time as the parties can bargain for a Special
Education article, there are a few items that should be adopted as a part of this CBA.
SDC
Based on the recommended caseloads for certain SDC classes in the expert special education report, if
the caseloads below are exceeded, the teacher shall receive $350 per month that their caseload is
exceeded.
Preschool 10 students
TK-8 Mod/Severe 12 students
TK-8 Mod/Severe Autism Focus 10 students
TK-8 Mild/Mod 15 students
2

RSP
Each full-time RSP teacher will have an Instructional Assistant assigned to the resource program to
support students for 6 hours per school day.
Toileting
Teachers are responsible for instruction, supervision, and the learning of all students in the classroom.
When teachers step away to assist with toileting, it interrupts instruction and supervision for the entire
class. Trained support staff are better positioned to handle toileting needs so teachers can remain
focused on teaching, maintaining a safe classroom environment, and supporting student learning.
The District shall designate non-certificated personnel as the primary provider of student diapering and
other toileting needs. If support staff are unavailable, the site administrator, classroom teacher, or
other designee shall be responsible for contacting the parent/guardian to provide assistance.
Finally, requiring an analysis on multi-year projections in our school district budgets produces many
problems for union members and for the stability students need from districts. Instead of a tool to
support realistic budgeting, we see year after year LLCSD under projecting revenue and over
projecting certain expenses which inherently favor the employer in thwarting collective bargaining
demands, resulting in unnecessary threats of cuts, layoffs, increases to class sizes, and the
manufactured crisis we are now experiencing.

Angela Su, LLEA Panel Member
