FACTFINDING PANEL REPORT- 13

Dissent and Partial Concurrence Regarding the TRUE-TRUSD Fact-Finding
Report, March 2, 2026
"Our mission isn't to save money, ... it is to create a stable environment. ... [C]lassroom teachers
instability causes them to constantly look around them as opposed to being focused on their
classroom."
Mike Fine, CEO California's Fiscal Crisis Management Assistance Team, February 26, 2026, Ed
Source Roundtable, "Teachers on strike: Can school districts in California afford what teachers
want?"
#
Instead of bringing the parties closer together, the fact-finder's report makes a strike
inevitable.
The fact-finder's report fails to address any of the serious concerns raised by educators,
takes no meaningful steps to ensure that Twin Rivers classrooms are fully-funded, and
recommends the continuation of the status quo that every day leaves two thousand Twin
Rivers Unified School District students without a permanent credentialed educator
providing instructional services.
The fact-finder's recommendation completely fails to address this crisis and makes no
contribution to averting the strike.
For the last six years, the District's outside independent auditor has cited TRUSD in its annual
audited report for its failure to comply with California Ed Code that requires unified school districts
to spend 55% of their annual budget on classroom staff. For six years, TRUSD has defied those
recommendations, diverting $116 million, or an average of over $19 million per year, away from
classrooms. The fact-finder was made aware of this non-compliance but her recommendation fails
to factor in those millions of dollars as statute requires her to con ·id r in order to fully fund
classrooms and address the concerns of students and staff.
TRUE has proposed numerous improvements, including lowering class sizes, reduced caseloads and
improved services for students with disabilities, overages for when class sizes and caseloads are
exceeded, an end to reliance on outside contractors, the reduction of unnecessary testing, the use of
Al, increased prep time for elementary teachers, an end to practices which expand educators' work
day without compensation, and protections for personal and academic freedom. The fact-finder's
recommendation addresses almost none of these proposals, recommending largely the status quo on
all articles except wages and medical insurance. And even in those limited areas where something
other than the status quo is recommended, the improvement is limited.
A full year after negotiations began, Twin Rivers educators represented by the Twin Rivers United
Educators (TRUE) believe that a contract negotiated with Twin Rivers Unified School District
1

should reflect the same significant improvements achieved by the Sacramento City Teachers
Association in June 2025, the United Teachers of Richmond in December 2025, the United
Educators of San Francisco in February 2026, the San Diego Education Association in February
2026, and the Oakland Education Association in March 2026.
Unfortunately, the neutral has chosen not to be informed by those agreements which establish and
consolidate new standards for educators across the state of California, thereby largely disregarding
applicable criteria, notably state law applicable to the employer and the interests and welfare of the
public and financial ability of the public-school employer. In her zeal to accept the austerity
arguments of the TRUSD, she even recommended a first-year salary increase lower than the
proposal TRUSD currently has on the table.
It is without argument that Twin Rivers Unified School District is
one of the strongest financially-positioned school districts in the
state of California. The fact-finder operates as if TRUSD is on the
verge of insolvency.
• TRUSD is One of the Small Number of Districts Where Enrollment/A DA is
Growing and Has the Second Highest Rate of Enrollment Growth for Comparable
Districts
Across California, 2/3 of all school districts are experiencing long-term enrollment decline.
Twin Rivers is an exception. From 2021-22 through 2024-25 for which data is available, out
of 44 unified school districts in California with an ADA of 20,000 students or more, Twin
Rivers is one of only eleven where enrollment has increased over the past five years. Out of
those 44 districts, Twin Rivers' enrollment growth ranks number five. The number of
students enrolled in Twin Rivers Unified has increased from 23,904 in 2021-22 to 25,164 in
2025-26, an increase of 1,260 students or 5.3%.
• TRUSD has failed to meet the Ed Code 41372 that unified school districts spend 55%
of their budget on classrooms since 2019-20, and is a massive outlier. The District
failed to address the fact that the failure in 2024-25 was the sixth year in a row that the
District failed to spend the required 55%, totaling $116 million since 2019-20 diverting the
money to its unrestricted reserve fund and its special Fund 40 (see below). The District also
failed to disclose that in each of those years, the District's own independent auditors
recommended that the District correct the deficiency, a recommendation that the District
repeatedly ignores. Of the 44 comparator school districts, TRUSD is one of only four that
failed to meet the requirement in 2024-25.
2

• TRUSD has one of the highest Unduplicated Pupil Populations (UPP) in the state,
resulting in LCFF funding that exceeds $3500 per student - higher than other
Sacramento County districts and the median of unified school districts with ADA
over 20,000 students. These funds are meant to improve outcomes of "high needs"
students including English Learners, low-income, and foster youth. The District has the
means to fill vacancies, retain educators, and reduce class sizes cuts for Sacramento's most
underserved students and families.
• TRUSD has failed to provide salary increases to certificated staff that have kept pace
with District LCFF revenue increases. Salary increases to the TRUE bargaining unit
salary schedules have not kept pace with the District's increase in LCFF revenue. Since
2020-21, the District's LCFF revenue has increased by a cumulative 35.3%, while salary
schedules have only increased by a cumulative 23.8%, a gap of 11.5%.
• TRUSD's unrestricted reserve fund exceeds the 10% maximum reserve fund
currently in effect for California school districts by $19.5 million. Based on the
District's most recent unaudited actuals, the District's current unrestricted reserve fund is
$73,094,573, or $19.5 million over the ten percent maximum, currently in effect. TRUSD
did not dispute this number.
• Over the past six years, TRUSD has diverted over $267 million in unrestricted
general fund dollars into special building Fund 40-the highest percentage of
comparable districts in the state, and second only to Los Angeles Unified School
District in actual dollars, a district that is approximately 24 times larger.
• TRUSD is failing to meet its stated goal of retaining 95% of certificated staff.
• TRUSD relies on outside contractors to a greater extent than comparable districts.
TRUSD's spending on "Services and Other Operating Expenses" has increased from
14.86% in 2020-21 to 19.59% in 2024-25, the third highest of comparable districts.
• The Governor's proposed 2026-27 California budget includes significant
improvements for school districts. For TRUSD, in addition to the COLA increase of
2.41%, the budget includes an additional $36,441,478 in revenue.
• The District operates every year on record with massive annual unrestricted
surpluses, all while it has and continues to divert millions of unrestricted dollars into
Fund 40. Instead of using these large unrestricted surpluses to meet its statutory
requirements of spending on education, the District instead has prioritized diverting $267
million in unrestricted general fund revenue into Fund 40. In the current year, the District is
3

budgeting additional Fund 40 contributions of $32.8 million in 2025-26, and $23.3 million in
both 2026-27 and 2027-28. The District's end of the year net unrestricted revenue
(Unrestricted revenue - unrestricted expenditures) from 2019-20 through 2027-28
(projected) is below, with supporting material in Appendix I.

• The District-provided data confirms that TRUSD spending on certificated
salaries dropped from 38.79% in 2019-20 to 35.41%.
• The District claims its current class size averages "are well under the current
requirements in the collective bargaining agreement," but refuses to agree to
a more standardized overage pay if those standards are not met.
• The District's total compensation is 34 th out of 44 comparable districts, and
$44,000 less in average total compensation compared to Sac City Unified,
which also operates in the City of Sacramento.
Despite these facts, the primary factor that appears to have driven the
fact-finder's recommendation is that the across-the-board increase
should be limited to the LCFF COLA increase for 2025-26 and 2026-27.
The recommendation does not take into account the repeated
recommendation from the District's independent auditor that it meet the
state required 55% spending threshold on classrooms, a
recommendation made every year by the independent auditor since 2019-
20.
4

Regarding the specific recommendations proposed by the fact-finder, TRUE offers the
following response:
Salary-Article 13.
The fact-finder recommends a 2.3% ongoing increase effective July 1, 2025, and 2.41 %
effective July 1, 2026.
The recommendation does not take into consideration the settlements reached in
Sacramento, Richmond, San Francisco, San Diego, and Oakland, particularly with the
average Twin Rivers educator earning $10,000 less per year than educators at adjoining Sac
City Unified.
!Additionall , it is lower than the 2.5% increase that is currently the District's year one

While the contribution for medical benefits based on the Kaiser HMO rates is a step
forward, recommending that this provision sunsets on the last day of the contract introduces
a totally unacceptable and unnecessary level of instability into the total compensation
package of TRUE educators particularly given TRUSD's strong financial position and the
fact that it provides folly-employer paid health insurance for Superintendent Steve
Martinez, TRUE DISSENTS.
Regarding the exclusion of dental and vision and the adjustment to retiree health: TRUE

For all of these issues, the fact-finder recommends the Status Quo, TRUE DISSENTS.
In simply recommending the status quo, the fact-finder rewards TRUSD for stonewalling

FACTUAL BACKGROUND
2
The Oakland Unified School District ("OUSD" or "District") is located in Oakland,
3
California and serves nearly 34,000 students and employs more than 3,000 educators in 84
4
schools consisting of 51 elementary schools, 11 middle schools, 11 high schools, 6 alternative
5
schools and 24 charter schools in addition to preschool programs, a Young Adult Program and a
6
7 Home to Hospital Program that serves students with a temporary illness or injury that makes
8
attending school impossible or inadvisable. Oakland, California draws students from a diverse
9
socio economic, ethnic, and linguistic background. Approximately 18% of the District students
in TK-12 are students with disabilities who receive special education services.
11
The District is a public school employer within the meaning of Section 3540.1 (k) of the
12
13 Educational Employment Relations Act ("EERA"). The Oakland Education Association
14
("OEA" or ''Association'') is the recognized employee organization within the meaning of
15
Section 3540.1 of the EERA and has been the duly recognized representative of 3000
16
certificated non-management members of the bargaining unit.
17
The parties' efforts to negotiate a successor collective bargaining agreement ended in
19 impasse after fifteen negotiating sessions. On November 6, 2025. The Association filed a
20
Request for Impasse Detem1ination and on November 14, 2025, PERB determined impasse
21
existed and assigned a mediator. On December 17, 2025, PERB released the parties to Fact
22
Finding and PERB appointed Cheryl Stevens as the neutral Fact Finder on January 20, 2025.
A. Financial Data
24
25 The evidence presented by the pat1ies is in dispute as to whether the District has the
26
financial means to pay the Association's proposed wage increase and other proposed contract
27
changes. The Association contends that it was unable to fully assess the District's financial
28
HEARING DATE: FEBRUARY 10, & 17. 2026-4

situation because it did not receive clear data and the information was constantly evolving,
2
making it difficult for the Association to determine exactly how much the District has available
3
to spend on wages and OEA's other demands.
4
The District explained that a 1% salary increase represents $2,747,000 for Association
5
members and $5,043,000 for all District employees. (District Exh. 1) The District reported more
6
7 than $837 million in operating revenues for 2024-2025. (District Exh. 4) Yet the ongoing
8
declining enrollment has significantly impacted the revenue it receives from the State. In fact,
9
the District's LCFF revenue did not increase with the COLA and as a result the District incutTed
10
significant deficit spending in 2024-2025 and the District's reserves declined significantly in
I I
2024-2025. Specifically, the District's LCFF revenues decreased by more than $9.4 million or
12
13 1.94% and was the primary reason there was no wage increase in 2024-2025. (District Exh. 8)
14
While there was significant decline in revenue, expenditures exceeded revenues by $61 million
15
requiring the District to spend 52% of its reserves in 2024-2025 and continued reduction in
16
revenues is expected for 2025-2026. (District Exh. 9) Although the Disu·ict was unable to fund
17
a wage increase in 2024-2025 based on the significant reduction in revenue, it still ranks fourth
18
19 among the comparative districts on personnel costs. (District Exh. 11) The District also ranks
20
fifth among the twenty (20) comparative districts on spending for Special Education,
21
representing 14.83% of its total expenses. (District Exh. 14)
22
The State requires school districts to maintain a minimum balance of 3 % of unrestricted
23
reserves. In 2023-2024, the District maintained a balance 13% compared to other unified district
24
25 in the State that maintained an average of 24.36 %. However, the District only maintained a
26
balance of 6.28% in 2024-2025. (District Exhs. 16 and 17) The District has $55,845,233 in
27
unrestricted reserves but $200,777,711 in restricted reserves and the District is prohibited from
28
HEARING DATE: FEBRUARY 10, & 17, 2026 -5

tapping into the unrestricted reserves to fund the contract changes. Moreover, the District
2
currently has a budget ce11ification status of ''qualified" that is contingent on the District's ability
3
to make significant budget cuts while avoiding new expenditure commitments. For that reason,
4
the District was reluctant to over commit its reserves or agree to increases that would be
5
inconsistent with the limits imposed on their qualified status.
6
7 B. Wage and Benefit Comparison
8
Another statuto1y criteria to consider is a comparison of the wages, hours and conditions
9
of employment of the employees involved in this Factfinding compared to the wages, hours, and
IO
conditions of employment of employees working in comparable positions and comparable
II
communities. OEA presented exhibits that compared their wages with ten other unified school

13 districts in the Bay Arca. Based on OEA 's comparison charts, their members are lowest paid
14
educators in the Bay Area. (OEA Exh. l) The District on the other hand relied on twenty
15
districts including the same ten districts in the Association's list of comparable districts;
16
hO\:vevcr, because many of the districts included in the District's list include school districts with

lower ADA and as a result Oakland ranks higher. Additionally, the District did not prepare a
18
19 direct comparison of wages; but instead compared salary and benefits per ADA as well as
20

21
Oakland at the top of the rankings but is not a true comparison of the wages paid to the
22
educators. Furthennore, including ten otherdistricts dilutes the findings improves OUSD's
23
financial profile. Accordingly, I think the Association's reliance on the ten neighboring unified
24
25 school districts for comparison purposes is a more accurate and appropriate comparison.

C. Non-Wage Related Issues
27
There were several non-wage related issues that were raised and discussed in detail on

the approach of consolidating staff associated with the Newcomers program. The Panel

have been made in this Recommendation to consider these proposals and their associated costs

along with the demand for wage increases to establish some balance between all of the

competing factors on the District's budget.
II
For example, the Association believes that reducing class size at the Kindergarten and
12
13 first grade levels will have a positive impact on increasing Oakland's literacy rate even if it

schools and will eventually relocate to charter schools or another district thus further reducing

20
20 students in a Kindergat1en or first grade class is better than 29 students creating a more

conducive learning environment that surely open doors for these students through literacy and
22
establish a stronger foundation. The benefits appear to outweigh the possible loss of revenue;

therefore, the Panel recommends reducing class size for K-1s t grade to 22 students.

26
Continuation schools and that the administration will notify the sites of any issues with a student

prior to placement. OEA wanted a cap of 25 on class size for Continuation schools but this did
28
HEARING DATE: FEBRUARY 10, & 17, 2026 -7

not appear to be a real problem necessitating this change at this time as the classes are usually
2
well below this cap.

Additionally, the parties were able to reach agreement regarding some of the issues
4
associated with the Newcomer program, a program that works diligently to provide support to

7 program has identified many competent educators committed to assisting this important

Finally, there were several non-wage related requests made for the Visual and Performin

Arts program. Chief among them included advance notice of budget allocation, identifying

and materials. OEA also asked that the TSAs assigned to V APA become codified positions
21
recognized in the CBA because the V APA educators believe their support to be invaluable to the
22
program. While not directly a wage-related request, incorporating the two (2) TSA positions int
23
the CBA creates a strain on the budget. First, it adds 2 positions to the budget and treats these

25 TSAs differently from other TSAs in the District. Second, instead of investing resources in the

27
from the students. The District's explanation for not codifying the VAPA positions was
28

reasonable and otherwise did not indicate these positions would be eliminated. Finally, the
2
District agreed to identitYing space for equipment and materials and working with the V APA
3
educators to identify appropriate performance space in an effort to demonstrate its support of this
4
very important educational tool.

DISCUSSION AND RECOMMENDATION
6
7 It is the role of the Panel to apply the relevant factors set f 011h in EERA, to the facts
8
underlying the impasse presented, and render its best recommendation considering those factors.
9
The factors that apply are discussed herein.
10
II
A. The Interests and Welfare of the Public and the Financial Ability of the Public
School
12
13 The parties disagree on whether the Association's proposed wage increase is in the
14
best interest and welfare for the conununity. The Association argues that the District's proposed
15
wages are not competitive; and when compared to the other ten neighboring districts, OEA
16
members arc at the bottom of the salary scale. The Association insists that if the District stopped
17
hiring outside consultants to perform bargaining unit and reduced the wage increases for
18
19 administrators there would be sufficient funds available in the budget to support a wage increase
20
for the educators. Furthem1ore, it is OEA 's position that a significant wage increase is necessary
21
not only to provide the teachers with a comparable wage but also to ensure Oakland students
22
receive the best education based on the quality of the teaching staff recruited and retained
23
because of the District offering competitive sala1ies.
24
25 Fmthermore, OEA reported that increasing salaries would minimize Oakland's high
26
attrition rate and reverse the ten-year trend of 400 educators leaving the District every year.
27
Although the true status of the District's current financial position is unclear, OEA believes that

PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND
On December 22, 2025, the United Public Employees (UPE) filed a request for
factfinding pursuant to the Meyers-Milias-Brown Act (MMBA) with the Public
Employment Relations Board (PERB or Board) regarding the County's proposed
reinstatement of a weekly feedback productivity report (weekly feedback report) within

the Department of Human Assistance (DHA), County of Sacramento (County). The
request included the Association's December 22, 2025 Declaration of Impasse which,
in effect, stated that UPE and the County could not come to an agreement on the
implementation of the proposed reinstatement of the weekly feedback reports.

APPLICATION OF STATUTORY CRITERIA AND RECOMMENDATIONS
Unlike interest arbitration, where a third-party neutral sets the terms of a
new agreement, a third-party neutral in an MMBA factfinding report simply provides
recommendation(s) as to terms for settlement, which shall be advisory only.
(Gov. Code,§ 3505.5, subd. (a).) In essence, the impasse resolution procedure,
which includes the factfinding process, is a continuation of the collective bargaining
process. (San Bernardino County Superintendent of Schools (2024) PERS Decision
No. 2934, p. 16.) Ultimately, the parties must persuade one another of their positions,
and the neutral factfinder simply provides an outside perspective to assist the parties
possibly to come to an agreement over matters within the scope of representation.
11

(City of Oakland (2018) PERB Order No. Ad--462-M, p. 4; County of Ventura (2018)
PERB Order No. Ad--461-M, p. 5.) Both parties to the factfinding process are
statutorily obligated to participate in this process in good faith. (San Bernardino
County Superintendent of Schools, supra, p. 16; County of Santa Clara (2020)
PERB Order No. Ad-483-M, pp. 5-6.)
Government Code section 3505.4, subdivision (d) states that factfinders shall
"consider, weigh, and be guided by" those criteria set forth in subdivisions (d)(1)
through (8). One of those criteria is Government Code section 3505.4,
subdivision (d)(4)-"[t]he interests and welfare of the public." DHA administers public
assistance benefits to eligible applicants of the public who qualify for such assistance.
It is in the interest and the welfare of the public that DHA has its HHS, Senior Office
Assistants and Office Assistants perform efficiently in the timely processing of
requests for assistance to those in the public who are in the greatest of need
whether determining the eligibility of an applicant for such benefits or troubleshooting
a problem of an existing recipient of benefits.
The County intends to improve its HSS's production by means of comparing
one HSS employee's task production with the average of the unit's task production
over a weekly period and for the Supervisor to use this report at the one-on-one
meetings to find ways to improve the HHS's quantitative performance. In other words,
the County is utilizing the weekly feedback report to attempt to correct issues of
"incompetency" or "inefficiency."
12

In arbitrations, establishing "incompetency" can be based upon a continuous
pattern of activity or inactivity.16 In State Civil Service appellate court precedent,
"inefficiency" generally connotes a continuous failure by an employee to meet a level
of productivity set by other employees in the same or similar position. (Bodenschatz
v. State Personnel Board (1971) 15 Cal.App.3d 775, where inefficiency was found
when comparing statistical data of the employee's productivity with other California
Highway Patrol officers performing like duties.)
As incompetency or inefficiency can be defined as a "continuous" failure rather
than an isolated or periodic failure of production, the use of a one-week period to
determine inefficiency when compared with the average of the unit seems an
insufficient sampling period, even for purposes of a corrective or coaching discussion.
A period of time greater than one week is needed to demonstrate incompetency or
inefficiency. Thus, UPE has a valid point as to the irrelevance of the use of a one
week production comparative for its HHS employees and the average of the unit's task
production. In the Chair's mind, a larger sampling period greater than one week
ehould be used as a comparative to establish the relevancy of the comparison.
Recommendation(s) for Settlement: Pursuant to Government Code
section 3505.4, subdivision (d)(4) as to the "interests and welfare of the public," the
Chair recommends that the County reinstate the weekly feedback report without the
"Average Regular Tasks Completed by Unit" column on a weekly basis. However, the
"Tasks Completed in Regular Hours," "Walk-in Tasks Completed by Unit," and the

February 5, 2026
I, Jennifer Saetern, representative for the Sacramento County Department of Human
Assistance and panel member of this factfinding proceeding, concur with the findings and
conclusion. However, I would like to offer clarification on one specific area.
The purpose of the weekly feedback reports is to provide staff with consistent, ongoing
input regarding their performance. lt is not the department's intention to rely solely on
these reports-nor on a single week of data-when evaluating matters that may lead to
disciplinary nction. Patterns of inactivity or inconsistencies are reviewed over a broader
period to ensure a fair and accurate assessment. Additionally, while feedback reports serve
as one metric in evaluating employee performance, they are not the only factor considered.
Supervisors and QNQC staff also conduct monthly call reviews and case reviews, which
contribute to a more comprehensive evaluation.
I also concur with the recommendation to provide the "Tasks Completed in Regular Hours,"
"Walk-In Tasks Completed by Unit," and "Average Regular Tasks Completed by Unit" on a
monthly basis in conjunction with the weekly feedback reports.

Concurrence Statement of Union Panel Member
PERB Case No. SA-IM-258-M
Factfinding Report and Recommendation
February 4, 2026
I, Stephanie McCall, representative of United Public Employees (UPE) and panel member of this
fact-finding procedure, concur with the Chair's recommendation.
Specifically, UPE agrees to recommend that the County provide the additional quantitative
production metrics-"Tasks Completed in Regular Hours," "Walk-in Tasks Completed by
Unit," and "Average Regular Tasks Completed by Unit"-on a quarterly basis.
Quarterly reporting offers a more stable and representative sampling of workload trends, reduces
the volatility inherent in weekly fluctuations, and provides employees with meaningful
comparative information without creating unnecessary administrative burden. This interval also
aligns with the union's longstanding position that production data should be contextualized,
accurate, and not used in a manner that misrepresents employee performance.
UPE also concurs with the recommendation that the County issue a memorandum to all
UPE-represented employees explaining the purpose of reinstating the weekly feedback reports
on a quarterly basis. Transparency regarding the intent and use of these reports is essential to
maintaining trust and ensuring that employees understand how the information will-and will
not-be used.
